'''Sir Peter Bernhard Hirsch''' {{postnominals|country=GBR|size=100%|FRS|HonFRMS}} (16 January 1925 – 12 September 2025) was a British metallurgist who made fundamental contributions to the application of [[transmission electron microscopy]] to metals.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.materials.ox.ac.uk/peoplepages/hirsch.html|title=Personal Homepages Professor Sir Peter Hirsch FRS Emeritus Professor Department of Materials Oxford Materials|archive-date=3 April 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120403234532/http://www.materials.ox.ac.uk/peoplepages/hirsch.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Wilkinson | first1 = A. J. | last2 = Hirsch | first2 = P. B. | doi = 10.1016/S0968-4328(97)00032-2 | title = Electron diffraction based techniques in scanning electron microscopy of bulk materials | journal = Micron | volume = 28 | issue = 4 | pages = 279–308 | year = 1997 | arxiv = 1904.05550 | s2cid = 118944816 }}</ref>

==Life and career==
Hirsch was born in Berlin on 16 January 1925; his parents divorced in 1934 and his father died two years later.<ref name=aip>{{Cite interview |last=Hirsch |first=Peter |title=Peter Hirsch |interviewer-last=Case |interviewer-first=Stephen|url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/31625 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250114132015/https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/31625 |archive-date=14 January 2025 |access-date=19 March 2025 |website=www.aip.org |publisher=American Institute of Physics |language=en}}</ref> Hirsch lived in Germany until 1939; he was one of hundreds of Jewish children that escaped Germany via the various ''[[Kindertransport]]'' missions that saved many such children from the impending dangers of World War II and [[the Holocaust]].<ref name=aip />

Hirsch attended Sloane Grammar School, Chelsea, and [[St Catharine's College, Cambridge]]. In 1946 he joined the [[Crystallography]] Department of the [[Cavendish Laboratory|Cavendish]] to work for a PhD on work hardening in metals under W. H. Taylor and [[William Lawrence Bragg|Lawrence Bragg]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kelly|first=Anthony|date=1 January 2013|title=Lawrence Bragg's interest in the deformation of metals and 1950–1953 in the Cavendish – a worm's-eye view|journal=Acta Crystallographica Section A|language=en|volume=69|issue=1|pages=16–24|doi=10.1107/s0108767312034356|pmid=23250056|issn=0108-7673|doi-access=free|bibcode=2013AcCrA..69...16K }}</ref> His doctoral research was funded by grants from the [[British Iron and Steel Research Association]], the [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (United Kingdom)|Department of Scientific and Industrial Research]], and a junior research studentship from St Catharine's College.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hirsch|first1=P.B.|last2=Kellar|first2=J.N.|journal= Proceedings of the Physical Society, Section B|title=An X-Ray Micro-Beam Technique: I - Collimation|year=1951|volume=64|issue=5 |pages=369–374|doi= 10.1088/0370-1301/64/5/301 |bibcode=1951PPSB...64..369H }}</ref>
He subsequently carried out work, which is still cited, on the structure of [[coal]], funded by the [[National Coal Board]] and a University of Cambridge research fellowship.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Hirsch |first=Peter B. |year=1954 |title=X-ray scattering from coals |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London, Series A |volume=226 |issue=1165 |pages=143–169 |bibcode=1954RSPSA.226..143H |doi=10.1098/rspa.1954.0245}}</ref>

In the mid-1950s, he pioneered the application of [[transmission electron microscopy]] (TEM) to metals and developed in detail the theory needed to interpret such images. He was a Fellow of [[Christ's College, Cambridge]] from 1960 to 1966 and was elected an Honorary Fellow of Christ's in 1978. In 1965, with [[Archibald Howie|Howie]], [[M.J. Whelan|Whelan]], Pashley and Nicholson, he published the text ''Electron microscopy of thin crystals''.<ref>P. Hirsch, [[Archibald Howie|A. Howie]], R. Nicholson, D. W. Pashley and [[M.J. Whelan|M. J. Whelan]] (1965/1977) Electron microscopy of thin crystals (Butterworths/Krieger, London/Malabar FL) {{ISBN|0-88275-376-2}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Hirsch | first1 = P. B. | last2 = Howie | first2 = A. | last3 = Nicholson | first3 = R. B. | last4 = Pashley | first4 = D. W. | last5 = Whelan | first5 = M. J. | last6 = Marton | first6 = L. | doi = 10.1063/1.3047787 | title = Electron microscopy | journal = Physics Today | volume = 19 | issue = 10 | pages = 93 | year = 1966 | bibcode = 1966PhT....19j..93H }}</ref> The following year he moved to Oxford to take up the [[Isaac Wolfson]] Chair in Metallurgy, succeeding [[William Hume-Rothery]], and was elected a Fellow of [[St Edmund Hall, Oxford]]. He held this chair until his retirement in 1992, building up the Department of Metallurgy (now the [[University of Oxford, Department of Materials|Department of Materials]]) into a world-renowned centre. Among many other honours, he was awarded the 1983 [[Wolf Prize|Wolf Foundation Prize in physics]]. He was elected to the [[Royal Society]] in 1963 and knighted in 1975.

Hirsch was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2001 for experimentally establishing the role of dislocations in plastic flow and of electron microscopy as a tool for materials research. His great-niece is the writer and broadcaster [[Afua Hirsch]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.sydneyoperahouse.com/festivals/antidote/digital/articles/cheat-sheet-afua-hirsch.html | title=Cheat sheet: Afua Hirsch }}</ref>

In March 2025, the University of Oxford department of materials held a symposium in honour of Hirsch, to mark his 100th birthday.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.alumni.ox.ac.uk/article/new-microscope-blessed-by-sir-peter-hirsch|title=New microscope blessed by Sir Peter Hirsch|date=19 March 2025|via=QUAD|access-date=18 September 2025}}</ref> Hirsch died after a brief illness on 12 September 2025, at the age of 100.<ref>{{cite web |title=Hall remembers Sir Peter Hirsch FRS |url=https://www.seh.ox.ac.uk/news/hall-remembers-sir-peter-hirsch-frs |website=St Edmund Hall, University of Oxford |access-date=15 September 2025 |date=15 September 2025}}</ref>
